summary:
What happens when an astronaut feels unwell millions of miles from Earth—and immediate medical guidance is unavailable?

Traditional health dashboards display numbers. AstroGuard goes further: it helps turn health information into informed action.

AstroGuard is a working astronaut health-support prototype combining physiological monitoring, historical NASA space-environment data, experimental AI, and a six-step Mission Health Navigator.

Our core innovation is the journey from symptom to structured medical handoff. Astronauts can report concerns, answer adaptive questions, explore relevant NASA research, receive explainable next-step guidance, and generate reports for medical review.

We also trained our own AI model to estimate breathing rate using PPG signals—potentially allowing wearable optical sensors to provide respiratory information without a separate breathing sensor. Our ExtraTrees model achieved a mean absolute error of 1.518 breaths/minute, approximately 30% lower than the evaluated baseline.

Built with Java, Spring Boot, Python, FastAPI, and React, AstroGuard integrates real research data, working AI inference, and interactive software.

As a research prototype, it does not provide medical diagnoses.

Our vision: astronauts should have more than health measurements. They should have an evidence-informed path from detecting a concern to preparing for medical action.
details:
AstroGuard — From Health Monitoring to Informed Action

The Problem: What Happens After an Astronaut Reports a Symptom?

Imagine an astronaut experiencing a persistent headache during a mission far from Earth.

A conventional health dashboard may display heart rate, oxygen saturation, and respiratory rate. Environmental sensors may provide additional measurements. But numbers alone do not answer the most important questions:

What information should the astronaut collect next? Which scientific evidence is relevant? And how should the situation be communicated to medical professionals when immediate assistance is unavailable?

During future deep-space missions, communication delays, isolation, and limited access to real-time medical consultation will increase the importance of crew medical autonomy.

The challenge is not simply collecting more health data. It is helping astronauts turn fragmented information into structured, understandable, and useful information.

AstroGuard addresses the gap between detecting a health concern and preparing for informed medical action.

Our Solution: An Integrated Astronaut Health Support Platform

AstroGuard is a working, interactive research prototype combining physiological monitoring, historical NASA space-environment data, guided symptom assessment, explainable next-step guidance, and experimental artificial intelligence.

Rather than functioning as another dashboard that only displays measurements, AstroGuard provides a structured workflow that helps users move from identifying a concern to preparing information for medical review.

The platform includes five main capabilities.

1. Interactive Physiological Monitoring

AstroGuard visualizes physiological measurements, including:

  • Heart rate
  • Pulse
  • Blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂)
  • Respiratory rate

The platform also includes an interactive human body explorer that provides additional information about physiological systems.

For demonstration purposes, AstroGuard uses historical physiological recordings from the PhysioNet BIDMC dataset. These are real terrestrial clinical measurements, not live astronaut data.

2. NASA Space Environment Monitoring

AstroGuard integrates historical environmental measurements from NASA's Open Science Data Repository Environmental Data Application (OSDR EDA), associated with the RR-1 mission.

The dashboard visualizes:

  • Carbon dioxide concentration (CO₂)
  • Temperature
  • Relative humidity

Environmental awareness is particularly relevant during space missions because cabin conditions can influence crew comfort and well-being.

AstroGuard clearly identifies these measurements as historical research data rather than real-time International Space Station telemetry.

NASA environmental data and PhysioNet physiological recordings are independent datasets. They are not presented as synchronized measurements from the same astronaut or mission.

3. Mission Health Navigator — Our Core Innovation

The Mission Health Navigator is what makes AstroGuard more than a traditional health-monitoring dashboard.

It guides users through a six-stage workflow:

Concern → Symptoms → Adaptive Follow-up → NASA Research Evidence → Explainable Next Steps → Medical Handoff

Consider an astronaut experiencing a headache during a long-duration mission.

Instead of simply displaying physiological measurements, AstroGuard helps the user document the concern, answer relevant follow-up questions, review related NASA research, and understand the reasoning behind conservative next-step guidance.

The process results in a structured record that can support subsequent medical review.

The Navigator uses reviewable assessment logic rather than relying on a generative AI model to produce diagnoses or treatment decisions.

Its purpose is to organize information and support communication, not replace medical professionals.

4. Structured Medical Handoff

After completing the Mission Health Navigator, AstroGuard generates a Medical Handoff Report.

The report includes:

  • Reported symptoms and concerns
  • Responses to follow-up questions
  • Relevant research evidence
  • Data sources and provenance
  • Explainable next-step guidance
  • Limitations and information requiring medical review

Users can preview the report within the application, export it as HTML, or print it to PDF.

This is one of AstroGuard's most important practical outputs.

A reported symptom is transformed into a structured, evidence-linked document instead of remaining scattered across multiple screens or conversations.

The system does not automatically contact medical personnel or transmit reports to external medical services.

5. Experimental AI: Estimating Breathing Rate from an Optical Signal

One of AstroGuard's key technical contributions is a machine learning model that we trained to estimate respiratory rate from photoplethysmography (PPG) signals.

Instead of requiring a dedicated respiratory signal as input, our model estimates breathing rate from PPG — an optical signal commonly collected by pulse oximeters and wearable health-monitoring devices.

PPG primarily reflects changes in blood volume, but breathing can also influence the shape and variation of the waveform.

Our approach explores how machine learning can identify these patterns to estimate breaths per minute.

This offers an interesting possibility for future space-health monitoring: an optical wearable sensor could potentially provide additional respiratory information without requiring a separate breathing-sensor input.

To investigate this approach, we developed a complete machine learning pipeline using real physiological recordings from the PhysioNet BIDMC dataset.

Our implementation includes:

  • 64-second PPG signal windows
  • 125 Hz sampling frequency
  • 8,000 signal samples per window
  • 25 engineered signal features
  • An ExtraTrees regression model
  • A Python FastAPI inference service integrated into AstroGuard

The AI Insights interface displays predicted respiratory rate, reference measurements, absolute error, and prediction freshness.

Experimental evaluation results:

  • Physiological recordings: 52
  • Evaluated waveform windows: 1,402
  • Mean Absolute Error (MAE): 1.518 breaths/min
  • Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): 2.325 breaths/min
  • R² score: 0.301
  • Evaluated baseline MAE: 2.163 breaths/min

Under the reported exploratory evaluation setup, the ExtraTrees model achieved approximately 29.8% lower mean absolute error than the baseline.

Unlike simply calling a pre-existing AI service, we implemented the feature-extraction pipeline, trained and evaluated the model, and integrated real inference into a working application.

Why this matters: Our experiment demonstrates a potential approach for extracting additional physiological information from optical signals already used in wearable monitoring.

The approach could contribute to future research on compact, multiparameter astronaut health-monitoring systems.

However, respiratory-rate estimation from PPG is an existing research area. Our contribution is the implementation, experimental evaluation, and integration of this approach into AstroGuard.

The current model was trained and evaluated using terrestrial clinical recordings rather than astronaut data. It has not been clinically validated or tested on live wearable hardware.

Technical Implementation: How We Built AstroGuard

AstroGuard is a functioning software prototype built with a modular architecture.

Backend — Java and Spring Boot

We developed REST APIs for processing replayed physiological and environmental data, supporting assessment workflows, and generating medical handoff information.

Frontend — React and TypeScript

The frontend provides interactive health dashboards, environmental visualizations, a human body explorer, the Mission Health Navigator, Medical Handoff Reports, and AI Insights.

Machine Learning — Python and Scikit-learn

Python, NumPy, Pandas, and Scikit-learn were used for PPG data processing, feature extraction, model training, and evaluation.

AI Inference — FastAPI

A dedicated Python inference service allows the application to process PPG windows and obtain respiratory-rate predictions from the trained ExtraTrees model.

Data Simulation — Python

We built a replay simulator that sends historical research measurements into the application, making it possible to demonstrate the system without physical sensors.

Development Tools — Git and GitHub

The source code and documentation are published in a public repository to support transparency and reproducibility.

No dedicated medical hardware is required for the current research prototype.

Creativity and Innovation: What Makes AstroGuard Different?

Most health dashboards show users what their measurements are. AstroGuard explores how to help them understand what to do next.

The project combines two complementary innovations: an explainable assessment-to-handoff workflow and an experimental approach for deriving additional physiological information from PPG.

Four design decisions distinguish AstroGuard.

1. From Passive Monitoring to Guided Action

AstroGuard does not stop at displaying heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, and environmental conditions.

Its Mission Health Navigator helps users document a concern, collect relevant information, review supporting evidence, and prepare a structured medical handoff.

This creates a demonstrable workflow from symptom reporting to organized information for subsequent medical review.

2. Explainability Instead of Black-Box Medical Advice

The platform provides links to relevant NASA research and reviewable explanations of its conservative next-step guidance.

It distinguishes user-reported symptoms from historical research measurements and experimental AI predictions.

The assessment workflow is based on transparent application logic rather than automatically generated medical diagnoses.

3. Extracting More Information from Existing Physiological Signals

Our experimental respiratory-rate model explores how PPG, an optical signal commonly used in wearable devices, can provide information about breathing.

Instead of requiring a separate respiratory waveform as input, the model extracts relevant features from PPG.

With additional validation, this approach could contribute to more compact and flexible multiparameter wearable monitoring systems.

4. A Working Integration of Research, AI, and Software Engineering

AstroGuard connects a Java backend, React frontend, Python simulation pipeline, NASA environmental research data, physiological recordings, and a trained machine learning model.

The result is not simply a conceptual presentation, dashboard mockup, or AI training notebook.

It is an integrated software prototype that demonstrates data processing, model inference, guided assessment, and medical handoff generation.

Demonstrated Results and Impact

AstroGuard already demonstrates several concrete technical capabilities:

  • Interactive visualization of physiological and historical space-environment measurements
  • Integration of real historical NASA OSDR environmental data
  • A complete six-stage guided symptom assessment workflow
  • Evidence-linked explanations and conservative next-step guidance
  • Generation of structured Medical Handoff Reports
  • A trained and experimentally evaluated respiratory-rate estimation model
  • Working integration of machine learning inference into the application

Our most important demonstrated outcome is the complete transition from a reported concern to a structured medical handoff.

For example, a user can begin with a headache scenario, provide symptom details, answer adaptive follow-up questions, review relevant NASA evidence, and generate a report containing the information collected throughout the assessment.

This demonstrates how fragmented health-related information can be organized into a consistent document for subsequent medical review.

Our machine learning component provides an additional measurable technical result.

Using historical PPG signals, the ExtraTrees model achieved a mean absolute error of 1.518 breaths per minute, approximately 29.8% lower than the evaluated baseline.

These results demonstrate technical feasibility within our experimental setup. They do not establish clinical effectiveness or operational reliability in spaceflight conditions.

Intended Impact: Supporting Medical Autonomy Beyond Earth

Future lunar and deep-space missions will require astronauts to manage more situations without immediate real-time assistance from Earth.

AstroGuard explores how software could help address this challenge.

For astronauts, a guided assessment workflow could support more consistent symptom documentation and help identify information that may be useful when medical assistance is delayed.

For medical professionals, structured handoff reports could provide clearer, more organized context about reported symptoms, assessment responses, and relevant research evidence.

For space-health researchers, AstroGuard provides an extensible prototype for studying how physiological monitoring, explainable assessment workflows, and experimental AI might work together.

For future wearable monitoring systems, our PPG-based respiratory-rate model demonstrates a possible approach for extracting additional physiological information from an existing optical signal.

With further validation, such methods could contribute to research on compact monitoring solutions that provide multiple physiological indicators from wearable sensing hardware.

The long-term goal is to investigate whether integrated systems of this kind can improve the clarity, completeness, and usability of medical information during missions with communication delays.

These potential benefits have not yet been established through astronaut studies, clinical trials, or operational spaceflight testing.

Our vision is a future in which astronauts are not left with just numbers on a screen, but have tools to understand their situation and prepare for informed medical decisions.

Responsible Design and Scientific Integrity

Because AstroGuard addresses health-related information, responsible design was a major consideration throughout development.

Our priorities include:

  • Medical safety: AstroGuard does not diagnose diseases, prescribe treatment, or replace qualified medical professionals.
  • Data integrity: NASA environmental records and PhysioNet physiological measurements are historical, independent datasets.
  • Traceability: The platform identifies the origins of research measurements, user-reported information, and experimental AI predictions.
  • Explainability: The Mission Health Navigator uses reviewable application logic and evidence-linked guidance.
  • Privacy: The current prototype is intended for demonstration and research. Real deployment would require authentication, secure persistent storage, and appropriate protection of medical information.
  • Validation: Our model requires further testing with representative populations, hardware, and operational conditions before medical use.
  • Extensibility: The modular architecture allows future integration with suitable sensors, additional research datasets, and improved assessment workflows.

AstroGuard is not NASA-approved, does not use live astronaut sensors, and has not been validated for operational medical use during space missions.

Future Development

Our next steps include:

  1. Collaborating with medical and space-health experts to review the assessment workflow and evidence-linked guidance.
  2. Conducting usability studies to evaluate the clarity, completeness, and practical value of Medical Handoff Reports.
  3. Validating the respiratory-rate estimation model on additional and more representative physiological datasets.
  4. Investigating integration with wearable optical sensors.
  5. Implementing authenticated access, secure persistent storage, and privacy protections.
  6. Testing the workflow under simulated deep-space communication delays.
  7. Exploring how additional physiological indicators could be derived from existing wearable sensor signals.

https://www.nasa.gov/reference/3-0-health-and-medical-care/

AstroGuard — From Health Monitoring to Informed Action

We are not simply building another dashboard for space.

We are developing and evaluating a system that helps transform physiological information and reported symptoms into structured, evidence-informed information for medical review.

By combining real NASA research data, a guided assessment workflow, medical handoff generation, and an experimentally trained PPG-based respiratory-rate model, AstroGuard demonstrates a practical foundation for investigating more autonomous and explainable astronaut health-support technologies.

Our ultimate goal is simple: help future astronauts move beyond monitoring toward informed action — even when Earth is far away.
